= Inventory of 1605: Katerine Glasgow and Deceased Uncle =  
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}  

== Biography ==  
This page presents a detailed research summary of a 1605 inventory likely linked to the Glasgow family, particularly to a woman named '''Katerine Glasgow'''. The inventory is dated 15 May 1605 and comes from the Glasgow Commissary Court (NRS Reference: CC7/7/4). While the full testament is not available, this analysis draws upon surviving excerpts and image snippets to reconstruct the individuals and circumstances mentioned.

* [[Glasgow-1495|Catherine (Glasgow) Weir (bef.1560-)]], spouse to Thomas Weir, in the parish of Steinstone

== Key Individuals ==

* '''Katerine Glasgow''' – Possibly the executor, testatrix, or related beneficiary.
* '''The Umquhile Vnceis''' – The deceased "uncle" whose estate is inventoried; his personal name is not given.
* '''Campbell''' – Katerine’s sister, listed as a creditor; first name unknown.
* '''Robert Campbell''' – Possibly a relation of Campbell; also a creditor.
* '''Adam Carmichael''' – Possibly appeared to testify or gather information on behalf of the process.
* '''James Iones''' – Provided information; may be a son or relative of Rice Iones.
* '''Elizabeth Iones''' – Daughter of Rice Iones and deceased wife of Bateman Sorant.
* '''Rice Iones''' – Father of Elizabeth Iones.
* '''Bateman Sorant''' – Deceased husband of Elizabeth's mother.
* '''John Skeoch''' – Possibly someone who held goods of the deceased.
* '''William Davis''' – Possibly involved in the transfer of assets.
* '''Robert MacKenzie''' – Creditor owed £20.
* '''Margrett Allansoun & her spouse''' – Creditors owed two young cattle ("nolt").
* '''Lord and Lady Semple''' – Creditors owed eight mares and fowls.
* '''Robert Scott''' – Witness who swore the inventory to be accurate.

== Inventory of Assets ==

=== In the Borne and Barnyard ===
* 40 bolls of meal  
* 5 bolls of bear (barley) and associated fodder – valued at £6  
* 6 bolls of oats  

=== Household Goods ("Plenishing") ===
* 2 cows ("twa boes")  
* Furniture and utensils ("abonement of the buird and utensilis") – value unspecified  

== Debts ==

=== Debts Owed ''By'' the Deceased (Dettis awand Out) ===
* £30 to Campbell (Katerine's sister) for barley  
* 30 shillings to Robert Campbell  
* £20 to Robert MacKenzie  
* 2 nolt to Margrett Allansoun and her spouse  
* 8 mares and fowls to Lord and Lady Semple  

'''Total Debts Owing''': £80 6s 8d

=== Debts Owed ''To'' the Deceased ===
* Not listed in the excerpt – stated as "Na dettis awand In"

== Financial Summary ==
* '''Total Value of Inventory''': £85 6s  
* '''Total Debts Owing Out''': £80 6s 8d  
* '''Remainder (restis awand be the defunct)''': £64 19s 4d  
  * This was to be ''"dividit in thre pairtis"'' (divided into three parts)

== Legal Process ==
* The inventory was attested in Edinburgh on 15 May 1605.  
* '''Robert Scott''' acted as the witness and swore under oath that the accounting was truthful, with no known fraud.  
* Signature: ''"In witness quhairof my signe and subscriptioun is adhibit..."''  
* Note: ''"Cautione fund"'' indicates security was provided.

== Research and Genealogical Significance ==
This record is significant for researchers of the Glasgow surname in early 17th-century Scotland. It offers:

* A documented connection between Katerine Glasgow and her sister Campbell  
* Evidence of property ownership and debts in or near Glasgow  
* Links to possible creditors and family networks including the Campbells, MacKenzies, and Allansouns  
* The surname's presence in the Commissary Court shortly before the widespread adoption of surnames as heritable identifiers  

== Next Steps for Research ==
* '''Obtain the full will/testament (CC7/7/4)''' to determine the uncle’s name and Katerine’s legal role  
* Investigate the Glasgow Commissary Court records for 1605 and surrounding years  
* Search for parish records in Glasgow and Ayrshire for baptisms, marriages, and deaths of the individuals named  
* Explore sasine records for possible property transactions  
* Review testament dative indexes for Glasgow families without written wills  
* Revisit this document if Y-DNA matches suggest a connection to later Glasgow lines

== Cautionary Notes ==
* This analysis is based on partial documents and image snippets.  
* Interpretation of 17th-century Scots handwriting is inherently uncertain.  
* Relationships are implied but not definitively proven.

Guide to Translating a 1605 Glasgow Testament in Secretary Hand
Introduction to Secretary Hand (Early 17th-Century Scotland)

In the 16th and 17th centuries, Scottish legal documents—such as wills (testaments) and court records—were commonly written in Secretary Hand. This was a stylized cursive handwriting developed for official writing, known for its loops and flourishes (Secretary hand - Wikipedia) (Reading older handwriting (palaeography) | Scotland's People). Many letters in Secretary Hand have shapes very different from modern handwriting (for example, a, e, r, s, t, etc.), which can make it look “odd” or hard to read at first (Reading older handwriting (palaeography) | Scotland's People). Clerks of the time often mixed styles, so a single line might include primarily Secretary Hand letters with a few italic or idiosyncratic letters scattered in (Reading older handwriting (palaeography) | Scotland's People). Despite these challenges, Secretary Hand was the standard in Scottish church and commissary courts (which handled wills) until it gradually gave way to modern style in the  eighteenth century (Reading older handwriting (palaeography) | Scotland's People).

(image) Example of early 17th-century Scottish Secretary Hand from a 1605 Glasgow Commissary Court testament (reference CCg/7/4). Note the distinctive letter forms (such as the long, ƒ-shaped s and the looped h) and the use of contractions like the squiggled line in “testament” (replacing the letters ament). The word “Inventar” (inventory) is written as a title midway through the text.

Tips for Reading and Transcribing Secretary Hand

Deciphering Secretary Hand takes practice. Here are some tips to help read and transcribe this style of handwriting:

Learn the Unusual Letterforms: Several letters consistently look different from modern script (Elizabethan secretary hand • FamilySearch). For example, e may resemble a curled loop; c can look like a twisted r; r often has a long tail or unconventional shape; s frequently appears in its long s form (ſ) which can be mistaken for an f; h typically has a distinctive looped ascender; and k may be very ornate. Identifying these key letters (e, c, t, r, s, h, k, etc.) in various words will greatly improve recognition (Elizabethan secretary hand • FamilySearch). Compare unknown words to known ones in the document to confirm letter shapes.

Recognize Archaic Characters: Secretary Hand still uses some characters from Middle English. The thorn (þ), which looks similar to a y, stands for the sound “th” (). Thus, words like “the” might be written as “ye” (using thorn + e) in the document. The long s (ſ) is used for s in many places; it looks like an f without a full crossbar (
A Secretary Hand survival guide | English Ancestors	). Another character you may encounter is the yogh (ȝ), resembling a curved 3 or tailed z, which in Scots words can represent a y or gh sound (
A Secretary Hand survival guide | English Ancestors	). Being aware of these will prevent misreading (for example, “ȝeir” is “year”).

Common Abbreviations and Contractions: Scribes often abbreviated frequently-used words to save space. A horizontal stroke or squiggle above a letter usually signifies omitted letters (often an m or n) (). For instance, “com̄d” with a curl over the m might stand for “command”, and “summa” (Latin for “sum” or total) might be written as “sum̄a” with a squiggled second m (). The word “testament” was commonly abbreviated as “testᷤt”, where a flourish on the last t replaces the missing ament (). Likewise, “that” might appear as “yᷝt” (thorn for th with a superscript t) (). Familiarize yourself with marks like ʃ (often an abbreviation for sh or sir), the ampersand (&) for “and” (), and superscript letters indicating shortened endings. When in doubt, check if an unfamiliar squiggle could be an abbreviation – context will help decipher it ().

Minimal Punctuation: Don’t be surprised by the lack of modern punctuation (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK). 17th-century legal manuscripts often run clauses together with little more than an occasional period or comma. Scribes might use a slash (/) or simple dot to separate thoughts, or begin a new line for a new section, rather than using commas and semicolons as we do today. As you transcribe, you’ll likely need to insert modern punctuation mentally (or in your transcription) to make sense of sentences. For example, “I do ordain and make this my last will and testament in manner following First I give and bequeath…” might appear as one long clause in the original. Break it into sentences only for clarity, since the original won’t always do so (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK).

Use Context and Comparison: If a word is hard to make out, look at the surrounding words and overall context (). Legal testaments have formulaic language; recognizing a phrase like “In the name of God Amen” or “being seik in body bot haill in mynd” from its general shape can confirm individual letters. Compare letters across the document: if you identify a particular word (e.g. “God” or the name “Johne”), use it as a key for that writer’s G, d, or J shapes elsewhere. And remember, spelling was not standardized – writers often spelled phonetically or inconsistently, so consider variant spellings of a word when deciphering (e.g. “decease” might be spelled “deceiss” or “deceis”). Patience and practice are essential – try not to get stuck on one perplexing word; move on and come back with fresh eyes.

Glossary of Common Terms in 1600s Scottish Wills & Testaments

Understanding the vocabulary is just as important as reading the letters. Early 17th-century Scottish testamentary documents blend Scots language and legal terminology. Here are some frequent words and phrases and their meanings:

umquhile (umq᷉) – Literally “whilom” or “erstwhile,” meaning the late or deceased. Used to refer to the person after death, e.g. “umq᷉ John Smith” = “the late John Smith” (glossary of archaic Scots terms U).

relict – The surviving spouse of the deceased, usually the widow. In Scots usage, relict specifically means a widow (female), though it can apply to either widowed spouse (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). For example, “Janet Brown, relict of umquhile John Smith” indicates Janet was John’s widow.

bairns – Children. A common Scots word for children (sons and daughters). You may see “bairnis” or “bairns” in the plural. For instance, “bairns’ part” refers to the children’s share of an estate (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People).

gear (geir) – Goods, property, or moveable effects. Often appears in the phrase “goods and gear” (“guidis and geir”) meaning personal possessions (glossary of archaic Scots terms G) (glossary of archaic Scots terms G). Household items, furniture, tools, etc., would be encompassed by “gear.”

guids/goods – Spelled “guidis” or “gudis” in Scots, it means goods (moveable property). This is usually paired with gear as above, essentially doubling the term for emphasis (“all the guidis and geir” = all the goods and chattels).

Testament testamentar – A will in which the deceased testator named their own executor. In Scotland this term indicates there was a valid will, as opposed to a court-appointed administration (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People). The document will include the person’s wishes (bequests) and an inventory.

Testament dative – An estate settlement without a valid will, where an executor is appointed by the court (often a close family member) (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People). Such a testament primarily consists of an inventory of the deceased’s assets and debts, since the person died intestate (without making a will). Many 17th-century Scottish testaments are of this type, with phrases like “given up by [Name], executor-dative decerned” (meaning the court has decreed [Name] to be executor for the estate).

intestate – Dying without a will (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People). If someone is described as intestate, their estate would be handled via a testament dative rather than a testament testamentar.

executor – The person responsible for carrying out the terms of the testament. In a testament testamentar, the executor is named by the testator (often phrased “nominates and constitutes [Name] my executor”). In a testament dative, the executor (often the relict or a child) is appointed by the court (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People).

cautioner – A surety or guarantor. In testaments dative, the court often required the appointed executor to have a cautioner who pledged to ensure the estate was administered properly (glossary of archaic Scots terms C). You might see a line like “John Smith, with James Brown as cautioner, became executor-dative to the umquhile Jane Doe,” meaning James Brown acts as guarantor for John Smith’s execution of duties.

inventar (inventory) – A detailed list of the deceased’s moveable goods, debts owed to them, and debts owed by them. Usually appears as “Inventar” or “Inventarie” as a heading before listing the items (glossary of archaic Scots terms I). The inventory assigns values to each item or category of goods.

Item – Latin for “also”, used to start each entry in a list. In wills and inventories, “Item” is repeated at the beginning of each new bequest or listed asset, functioning like a bullet point (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK). For example: “Item, ane brood meir (one brood mare) price xx lib; Item, twa young oxen…” and so on.

Summa – Latin for “sum” or “total”. Appears at the end of an inventory to give the total value of the estate’s moveable goods (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). Often phrased as “Summa of the Inventar” or “Sum of all is” followed by the total in pounds, shillings, pence. (e.g. “Summa of this Inventar £240”). Sometimes written as “Totall” or abbreviated with a special symbol, but “Summa” is very common in 17th-century Scottish inventories.

quot (quotum) – A fee paid to the court for confirming the testament. In Scottish commissary courts, the quot was typically one-twentieth of the movable estate’s value (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People). You may see a note of “quot” or “quota” at the end of a testament (e.g. “quot paid” or “quota nulla” if the fee was waived for small estates).

(Note: Older Scots spellings vary – e.g. “quhilk” for “which,” “sedule” for “schedule,” “devyde” for “divide.” When in doubt, check the [Dictionary of the Scots Language] (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People) for unfamiliar terms.)

Scots, Latin, and English: Language Mixture in the Document

A 1605 Glasgow testament will exhibit a blend of Scots vernacular, standard (early modern) English, and Latin. Scottish testaments of this era were recorded in the Scots language – which is closely related to English but has its own vocabulary and spelling conventions – with Latin used for certain formalities and legal terms. Interpreting the document requires recognizing which language a word is in, as the clerk could switch mid-sentence.

Scots Vocabulary and Spelling: Much of the narrative and inventory will be in Scots. This includes common words like “seid” (seed), “meir” (mare), “buik” (book), or phrases like “haill guidis and geir” (whole goods and gear). Scots spelling can appear irregular to modern eyes, often phonetic – for example “buryit” for buried, “sowmes” for sums, “deceist” for deceased. Plural nouns frequently end in -is (or -es) in Scots, so “debts” might be written “dettis”, and past-tense verbs often end in -it (e.g. “nominat” for nominated) (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). Be aware that some Scots words are unique (like “umquhile” as above, or “lawful bairns” meaning legitimate children). Consulting a Scots glossary or dictionary is helpful for terms that are unfamiliar.

Latin Phrases and Legal Terms: Certain parts of the testament use Latin, reflecting the ecclesiastical legal tradition (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). Dates are commonly given in Latin: for instance, the document might say “the viij day of August, the yeir of God 1605” or even fully Latinized “Anno Domini 1605, mensis Augusti die octavo” (in the year of our Lord 1605, 8th day of August). In some cases, Scottish clerks wrote the year as “Jajvj°” or “jajviC” to represent 1600, followed by additional numerals for the year (). For example, “the year of God 1600 and eleven years” means 1611 (), and “In anno 1600 threescore one” would mean 1661 (with anno being Latin for "year" and the rest in Scots) (). Latin terms like “In Dei nomine, Amen” (In the name of God, Amen) might begin the will, and words such as “testamentum”, “vicarium”, or “quondam” (another term for late, similar to umquhile) may appear. Summa (total), libra/solidus/denarius (L, S, D) for currency, “Item” (as mentioned, Latin for "also"), and “et” (and) could be sprinkled in (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). Understanding basic Latin phrases or having a Latin word list can be very useful.

Standard English Influence: By 1605, Scots and English were mutually intelligible to a large degree, and scribes sometimes used English forms or spellings interchangeably. You might notice relatively standard English words or phrases especially if the clerk chose a more formal register. For instance, phrases like “I commend my soul to God” or “I nominate my spouse as executrix” are essentially English (with maybe minor spelling differences like “saule” for soul). This occasional use of standard English forms means a modern reader will catch some familiar words amid the Scots. However, the grammar might still reflect Scots usage (such as “the said” appearing as “the saidis” when plural (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People), or use of “the foresaid” (aforementioned) frequently). When translating, interpret in context: a word that looks like English might have a broader or slightly different meaning in Scots. For example, “gear” in Scots (as noted) means all sorts of belongings, not just mechanical gear.

In summary, expect a tapestry of languages: the structure and many key terms are Latin, the everyday words and phrasing are Scots, and some neutral terms could be essentially English. To interpret correctly, leverage all clues: if a phrase is opaque, determine if it might be Latin (then translate it) or a Scots colloquialism (check a Scots dictionary). Often, legal boilerplate was reused, so comparing with other wills of the period (or examples from guides) can shed light on meaning.

Partial Transcription and Translation of the 1605 Document

Below is a short excerpt from the 1605 testament (pictured above), transcribed in its original wording and then translated into modern English. This demonstrates how to apply the above tips in practice. (Ellipses […*] indicate portions not fully legible or skipped for brevity.)

Original Text (Transcription):
In the name of God Amen. I Johne Andersone in Gorballis, being seik in bodie bot haill in mynd and memorie, laud be to God, makis and ordanis my last will and testament as follows. Item, I commend my saule to God Almichtie my Creator, and my bodie to be bureit in the paroche kirk yard of Glasgow. … Thairfor I nominate my wife Elspeth Thomson my only executrix and intromissatrix with my guidis and geir. The Inventar: Item, the haill guidis, geir, sowmes of money and dettis pertaining to the deceissit, upon the ground of his dwelling, estimate to the availl (value) of £240. Summa of this Inventar foirsaid — ijc and fourty pundis (£240).

Modern Translation:
“In the name of God, Amen. I, John Anderson in Gorbals, being sick in body but whole in mind and memory (praise be to God), do make and ordain my last will and testament as follows. Item, I commend my soul to Almighty God my Creator, and I direct that my body be buried in the parish kirkyard of Glasgow. … Therefore, I nominate my wife, Elspeth Thomson, as my sole executrix and the one who shall manage (intromit with) my goods and gear.” The Inventory: “Item, the whole goods, gear, sums of money and debts belonging to the deceased, on the grounds of his dwelling, estimated to the value of £240. Total of this aforesaid Inventory – two hundred and forty pounds.”

Notes on the Example: In the original, you can see the standard preamble “In the name of God Amen” at the start, followed by the testator introducing himself and his condition “being seik in bodie bot haill in mynd” (HORNE, Francis (?-1653) – A 17th-century resident of Badsey | The Badsey Society) – a formula to assure he may be ill but is of sound mind. He then commends his soul to God and body to burial, which is typical of the religious sentiments expected in wills of this period (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK). The term “intromissatrix” (feminine form of intromitter) is a legal term indicating one who will administer the goods (we translated it as “manage” the goods and gear). The inventory section is introduced by “The Inventar”, and each asset line would begin with “Item,” though in this excerpt we combined them for brevity. The value “ijc and fourty pundis” is how the scribe wrote 240 pounds – “ijc” meaning two hundreds (200) and forty pounds, using Roman numeral notation for 200 (ijc, where j = 1 in old Scottish notation and c = 100) (). We rendered that simply as £240 in the translation.

When performing your own transcription, always keep the original spelling in the transcribed version (expanding abbreviations with brackets if needed), and provide a separate translation to modern English meaning. This allows you to preserve the historical text but also convey the content clearly to present-day readers.

Structure and Formulaic Phrases in Scottish Testaments

Scottish testaments of the early 1600s generally follow a predictable structure and use set phrases. Recognizing these patterns can greatly aid translation:

Opening Invocation: Almost every will begins with “In the name of God, Amen.” (HORNE, Francis (?-1653) – A 17th-century resident of Badsey | The Badsey Society) This is a standard invocation. It is typically followed by a clause stating the date and the testator’s name, residence, and condition, e.g., “the day of August 1605, I, John Anderson in Gorbals,… being seik in bodie bot of perfyte mynd and memorie, lauded be God, doe mak my testament.” The phrasing “being sick in body but of perfect mind and memory (praise be to God)” is very common (HORNE, Francis (?-1653) – A 17th-century resident of Badsey | The Badsey Society) (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK) – it establishes that the person, though ill, is mentally competent to make a will.

Commendation of Soul and Body: After introducing themselves, testators usually commend or recommend their soul to God and their body to be buried in a specific place. For example: “I commend my soul to Almighty God and my body to be buried in the parish churchyard of X.” (HORNE, Francis (?-1653) – A 17th-century resident of Badsey | The Badsey Society) Even if you can’t read every word of this part, knowing this convention helps – if you see “saule” and “bodie to be bureit,” you can guess the rest is the burial location. The burial place might be a “kirkyard” (churchyard) or other specified location, and sometimes with a desire for a “decent” or “honorable” burial, but the wording is formulaic.

Nomination of Executors: The will portion will state who is to execute the deceased’s wishes. Look for phrases like “I nominate and constitute” or “I mak and ordane” “X as my executor/executrix”. In our example, “I nominate my wife... my only executrix” is the key line. Sometimes multiple executors or substitute executors are named, and often identified by relationship (“my brother James”, “my eldest son John”, etc.). In intestate cases (testament dative), instead of the deceased nominating someone, the document (written by the court) will say “given up by [Name], executor-dative of the defunct, decerned by the Commissary”, indicating the court has appointed an executor. That is a standard legal phrasing for dative testaments.

Bequests (Legacies): In a testament testamentar (with a will), the testator may list specific bequests to individuals. Each of these usually starts with “Item” (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK). For example: “Item, I leave to my daughter Marione ane heifer of two yeiris auld” or “Item, I bequeath to my brother Robert my best suit of clothes.” The word “Item” here just means “Also,” indicating a new clause. Pay attention that people are often described by their relationship and sometimes their abode or occupation for clarity. Common wording for bequests: “I leave (or bequeath)… to …” and sometimes “for the help of” or “in token of my love,” etc. Many Scottish wills are short on personal messages and stick to naming the item and the beneficiary. If the will is long, it may number many “Item” clauses – transcribing each “Item” line by line is the best approach.

Residual Clause: Frequently, after listing particular legacies, a will has a catch-all clause for the remainder of the estate. For instance, “I give and dispone (dispose) the rest of my goods and gear to my wife, whom I make sole executrix.” In Scots wills, this might be phrased as “the rest of the guidis not particularlie bequeathed, I leave to…” or encompassed in the appointment of the executor (assuming the executor, often the spouse, gets what’s left after debts and specific bequests).

Inventory of Goods: Whether or not there was a will, an inventory of the deceased’s moveable property is compiled. It usually comes after the will text (often under the heading “Inventar” or simply introduced by “Item” once the narrative shifts). The inventory can be as brief or detailed as circumstances warrant. Often it groups goods into broad categories rather than itemizing every object. Typical inventory entries:

“Item, insicht geir within the house, estimat to £X” – “insight gear” means household goods (furniture, utensils, linens, etc.).

“Item, utencilis and domicilis, £Y” – another term for household stuff (utensils and domiciles).

“Item, crop of corn and bear (barley) upon the ground, valued to £Z.” – the grain crop in the fields.

“Item, nolt and sheep (cattle and sheep), worth £W.”

“Item, debts awand in (owed in) to the deceased by A, £…; Item, debts awand furth (owed out) by the deceased to B, £….” – money owed to the dead and money the dead owed others, respectively. These sections show credits and debits. Sums owed by the deceased might be subtracted from the total estate, while sums owed to the deceased are added.

Each line is prefaced by “Item” and ends with a valuation. The word “estimate” or “avail” (value) often appears: e.g. “estimate to the availl of ten pundis.” The values are given in pounds, shillings, pence (librae, solidi, denarii) of Scots money. You might see abbreviations like lib or li for pounds, s (or sh) for shillings, d for pence, or a combination of Roman and words (e.g. “xx lib vj s viij d” for £20, 6s. 8d., since vj is 6 and viij is 8). By convention, transcribe these exactly as written, then translate to modern £.s.d. notation or decimal currency in brackets if needed.

Summa (Total): After listing the assets (and sometimes after listing debts), the clerk will record the total value of the movable estate. This is introduced by a phrase like “Summa of Inventar” or “Sum of all the foirsaid”. For example: “Summa of the Inventar foresaid, £240 13s 4d.” (Unfamiliar words and phrases | Scotland's People). If debts owed by the deceased were listed, there may be a calculation where they subtract those and then say something like “Free geir (free gear) remaining, £___” after debts. The quot (confirmation fee) might be noted as well, e.g. “quot is xx s” or “quota nulla” (no quot due) (Introduction to Testaments Dative - Vocabulary | Scotland's People), though this is sometimes in the margin.

Confirmation Clause: Lastly, the record usually notes when and by whom the testament was confirmed. A line might read: “This testament was confirmet be the Commissary of Glasgow upon the 10th day of March 1606”. This indicates the court’s official approval (which could be months or years after the death). It’s often at the very end, sometimes in Latin (e.g. “Confirmatum fuit hoc Testamentum…”).

By understanding these standard components, you can navigate a testament document more easily. The phrases like “In the name of God Amen”, “being sick in body but hail of mind”, “I nominate X my executor”, “Item”, “Summa of inventar”, etc., are repeated across many wills (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK) (Reading wills and inventories | Tracing Ancestors In The UK). So, when you see a flourish of difficult handwriting, knowing that it likely says “I commit my soul to God and body to earth” or “given up by the relict as executor-dative” gives you a huge head start in deciphering it. Use this knowledge of formulaic language together with the paleography tips to decode your 1605 document step by step.

Familiarizing yourself with these standard forms and terms will make the process of translating a 17th-century Scottish testament much more approachable. Good luck with your transcription!
